title: Will, might, won't: talking about chance

summary.text: Close your eyes and pick one folded chit from a cup. Will it be red? For one cup the answer is 'it will'. For another it is 'it won't'. For a third cup nobody can tell, and the answer is 'it might'. You will test three cups, toss a coin like a cricket captain, and sort the things in your day into will, might and won't. You will also find out that 'might' can change when someone peeks.
summary.art: A girl with her eyes shut reaching into a steel tumbler of folded paper chits, with two more tumblers beside it on a kitchen floor.

intro.hook: You pick one chit without looking. From which cup will you get red for sure?
intro.text: Cup A. Every chit in cup A is red, so you will pick red. Cup C has no red chit, so you won't pick red. Cup B has both colours. From cup B you might pick red, and you might not. Nobody can tell before you pick. In this lesson you will test all three cups yourself. You will learn three words for what comes next: will, might and won't.
intro.art: Three steel tumblers in a row, tipped so we can see folded chits with red and blue dots inside.

outcomes: I can say if a thing will happen, might happen or won't happen.
I can give the reason, by looking at everything that can come out.
I can say that when a thing might happen, nobody can tell what comes this time.
I can change a cup so that 'won't' becomes 'might', or 'might' becomes 'will'.
I can use will, might and won't for things in my day, like the Sun, rain and dinner.
I can say that 'might' depends on what a person knows.

terms.meaning: Chance is about things that can happen in more than one way, when we cannot tell which way it will go this time.
terms.example: You toss a coin. It can land heads or tails. Which one you get is chance.
terms.art: A coin in the air above an open hand, with a small 'heads?' and 'tails?' beside it.

terms.meaning: It is sure to happen. Grown-ups also say 'certain'.
terms.example: Every chit in the cup is red. You will pick a red chit.
terms.art: A cup holding only red chits and a hand lifting one red chit out.

terms.meaning: It cannot happen. Grown-ups also say 'impossible'.
terms.example: A dice has the numbers 1 to 6. You won't roll a 7.
terms.art: A dice with its six faces drawn flat, and a crossed-out 7 beside it.

terms.meaning: It can happen, and it can also not happen. We cannot tell which this time. Another word is 'maybe'.
terms.example: The cup has red chits and blue chits. You might pick red.
terms.art: A cup with red and blue chits and a hand hovering above it with a question mark.

terms.meaning: You are sure when there is no other way it can go.
terms.example: You are sure the Sun will set this evening.
terms.art: A child pointing at a low orange Sun over rooftops.

terms.meaning: To say what you think will happen before you find out. A good guess comes with a reason.
terms.example: You say, 'I think it will be blue, because I see only blue chits.'
terms.art: A child looking into a cup of blue chits with a thought bubble showing a blue chit.

terms.meaning: To take one thing out with your eyes shut, so that you do not know which one you will get.
terms.example: You shut your eyes, shake the cup and take out one chit.
terms.art: A child with eyes shut, one hand in a steel tumbler.

terms.meaning: A small folded piece of paper with something marked inside.
terms.example: Families often write names on chits and pick one to choose whose turn it is.
terms.art: Four small folded paper chits, one of them open and showing a red dot.

terms.meaning: To flip a coin into the air and see which side lands up: heads or tails.
terms.example: Before a cricket match, the two captains toss a coin.
terms.art: Two children in a lane, one flipping a coin, with a bat and ball on the ground.

terms.meaning: This word goes past Class 1. A thing is likely when it might happen and usually does.
terms.example: The cup has 5 red chits and 1 blue chit. Red is likely.
terms.art: A cup with five red chits and one blue chit.

explanations.concept: Three words for what comes next
explanations.context: This card gives the three words you used in the Three Cups Test: will, might and won't.
explanations.definition: A thing will happen if it is sure. It won't happen if it cannot happen. It might happen if it can go either way.
explanations.description: Look at the three cups in the picture. Cup A has only red chits. You pick one without looking, and it will be red. Cup C has only blue chits, so your chit won't be red. Cup B has both colours. Your chit might be red. Now try it with a plate of only idlis. Will you pick an idli?
examples: The Sun will set this evening.
It might rain today.
You won't wake up taller than a coconut tree.
explanations.art: Three cups labelled will, might and won't, with red chits, mixed chits and blue chits.

explanations.concept: Look at everything that can come out
explanations.context: This card shows how to choose between will, might and won't. You look at all the things that can come out.
explanations.definition: First find everything that can come out. If all of them are what you want, it will happen. If none of them is, it won't. If only some are, it might.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. A dice has six faces: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Nothing else can come up. Will you roll a number smaller than 7? All six faces are smaller than 7, so you will. No face shows 8, so you won't roll an 8. Will you roll a 3? One face shows 3 and five faces do not, so you might.
examples: A coin has two sides. It might land heads. It won't land on a 5.
A box has only laddus. You will pick a laddu.
A spinner that is red all over will stop on red.
explanations.art: A dice unfolded so that all six faces show, with a tick beside 'smaller than 7' and a cross beside '8'.

chart.title: The six faces of a dice

explanations.concept: Might means nobody can tell this time
explanations.context: In the Three Cups Test you picked ten times from the cup with both colours. This card says what you found.
explanations.definition: When a thing might happen, you cannot tell what you will get on the next try. You find out only by trying.
explanations.description: From the mixed cup, red came on some picks and blue on others. The order was jumbled. The picture shows one child's ten picks. Yours will look different. You put the chit back each time, so the cup is just the same on every pick. If you got blue three times, the next pick still might be blue.
examples: A coin landed tails twice. The next toss might be tails again.
Two children test the same cup. Their picks come in a different order.
You say 'it might rain'. Then you watch the sky to find out.
explanations.art: A row of ten opened chits in a jumbled order of red and blue.

chart.title: One child's ten picks from the mixed cup

explanations.concept: One chit can change the answer
explanations.context: In the Three Cups Test you changed a cup of blue chits so that red might come. This card says how.
explanations.definition: Will, might and won't depend on what is in the cup. Change what is in the cup, and the answer can change.
explanations.description: A cup has 6 blue chits. You won't pick red. Now drop in one red chit. Red might come. One chit was enough to turn 'won't' into 'might'. To make it 'will', every chit must be red. So you take out all the blue chits. Shaking the cup harder or wishing changes nothing.
examples: A plate has only dosas. Put one idli on it. Now you might pick the idli.
A week with no holiday: add one, and a day off might be tomorrow.
A spinner is white all over. Colour one part red. Now it might stop on red.
explanations.art: A hand dropping one red chit into a cup of blue chits.

explanations.concept: Might for you, sure for someone else
explanations.context: In the Closed Hand step, a grown-up peeked at a chit and you did not. This card asks what that tells us about 'might'.
explanations.description: The grown-up picked a chit from the mixed cup and peeked. For you, the chit might be red. For the grown-up it was sure. It was the same chit. So 'might' can depend on what a person knows. Is every 'might' like this? People do not agree.
examples: Amma has wrapped your birthday present. For you it might be a book. Amma is sure.
The weather office has pictures of the clouds from space. They know more about today's rain than you do.
Before a toss, nobody knows how the coin will land. Not even the one who tosses.

perspectives.who: Pierre-Simon Laplace, a French mathematician, in 1814
perspectives.explanation: He wrote that someone who knew everything about the world at one moment would be unsure of nothing. So 'might' only shows what we do not know yet.
They say some things are a real 'might'. Take one tiny atom of the metal uranium. It can break apart at any moment. They say nobody could tell when, even with all the facts.

explanations.art: A grown-up peeking into her cupped hand with a small smile while a child looks on, a question mark above the child.

chart.title: One chit in a closed hand

explanations.concept: Will, might and won't in the sky
explanations.context: This card uses will, might and won't for the Sun, the rain and the night sky.
explanations.definition: Some things in the sky are sure. Others are a 'might' that even experts cannot turn into 'will'.
explanations.description: The Sun will rise tomorrow. The Earth is a big ball that turns round once every day, and it does not stop. Will you see the Sun rise? You might, because clouds can hide it. Will it rain tomorrow? In India the weather office studies the clouds and the wind. Even so, its reports often say rain is 'likely' or 'very likely'. Those are careful ways of saying 'might'.
examples: Night will come after this day.
You might see a shooting star tonight.
The Moon won't fall into your garden.
explanations.art: A child at a window at dawn, the Sun half hidden by a monsoon cloud.

explanations.concept: Other living beings weigh chances too
explanations.context: This card is about kea, who are parrots from New Zealand, and a test of how they deal with 'might'.
explanations.description: In 2020 two scientists, Amalia Bastos and Alex Taylor, tested six kea. The kea had learned that a black token gets a treat and an orange token gets nothing. Then they saw two jars, one with more black tokens and one with more orange. A person took one token from each jar and hid each in a closed hand. The kea had to touch one hand. They mostly chose the hand from the jar with more black tokens. Scientists do not agree on how much this tells us.
examples: The kea could not see the hidden token. They could only see what was in each jar.
It is like choosing between a cup with 5 red chits and a cup with 1 red chit.
Only six kea were tested, and all six live in a wildlife park.

perspectives.who: The scientists who did the test
perspectives.explanation: The kea looked at what was in each jar and picked the better chance. That is thinking about 'might', and they did it without words.
Six trained birds are very few. Nobody has yet shown how kea in the wild use this. It is safer to say that these six kea chose the better jar in this test.

explanations.art: A green kea parrot on a table reaching their beak toward one of two closed human hands, with two jars of black and orange tokens behind.

chart.title: Dark tokens get a treat. Which jar would you choose?

explanations.context: This card goes past Class 1. It is for a child who finds will, might and won't easy.
explanations.definition: Not every 'might' is the same size. A thing is likely if it might happen and usually does. It is unlikely if it might happen but usually does not.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. A cup has 5 red chits and 1 blue chit. Red might come, and blue might come. But there are many more red chits. So red comes much more often. We say red is likely and blue is unlikely. Unlikely is not 'won't'. The one blue chit is in the cup, and some day you pick it.
examples: In July in Kochi, rain is likely.
In May in Chennai, rain is unlikely. It still might rain.
A cup with 3 red and 3 blue: red and blue come about equally often.
explanations.art: A cup with five red chits and one blue chit, the blue one half hidden at the bottom.

agreed.text: If every chit in a cup is red, you will pick red every single time.
agreed.evidence: You tested it with cup A. There was no other colour that could come out.

agreed.text: If no chit in the cup is red, you won't pick red, however many times you try.
agreed.evidence: You tested it with cup C. You cannot take out what is not there.

agreed.text: When a cup has both colours, nobody can tell which colour comes next.
agreed.evidence: Your ten picks from cup B came in a jumbled order. Cricket captains trust a coin toss for the same reason: neither of them can tell how it will land.

agreed.text: Some birds choose the jar that gives them the better chance of a treat.
agreed.evidence: In a test in 2020, six kea parrots mostly chose the hand that came from the jar with more treat tokens (Bastos and Taylor).

challenging.claim: I got blue three times, so red must come next.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake people make with 'might'.
challenging.for: It feels as if red is waiting for its turn.
challenging.against: You put the chit back each time. So the cup is just the same on every pick. The next pick might be blue again.

challenging.claim: If a thing has never happened, it won't ever happen.
challenging.context: This card is about the difference between 'I have never seen it' and 'it cannot happen'.
challenging.for: If something has never been seen in a very long time, it is fair to guess it will not happen tomorrow.
challenging.against: Long ago, people in Europe had seen only white swans. A Roman poet, Juvenal, wrote of 'a rare bird, like a black swan'. He meant a thing nobody had ever seen. In 1697 a Dutch captain, Willem de Vlamingh, and his crew saw black swans on a river in Australia. 'Never seen' was not the same as 'won't'.

challenging.claim: Nothing is really 'might'. If we knew everything, we would always say will or won't.
challenging.who: Pierre-Simon Laplace, a French mathematician, in 1814
challenging.context: This card is about an old question: is 'might' in the world, or only in what we know?
challenging.for: In the Closed Hand step, the one who peeked was sure. More knowing made the 'might' go away.
challenging.against: Many physicists today say some things cannot be known ahead by anyone, such as the moment when one atom of uranium breaks apart.

big_questions.q: A cup has 100 blue chits and 1 red chit. Is picking red a 'might' or a 'won't'? Why?
big_questions.hint: Is the red chit in the cup? Can a hand reach it?

big_questions.q: You say 'it might rain' and it does not rain. Were you wrong?
big_questions.hint: What did 'might' promise? What did it not promise?

big_questions.q: Can you think of anything that will surely happen tomorrow? How do you know?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Sun, the day's name, your own breathing.

big_questions.q: When someone peeks at the chit, does the chit change, or does the person change?
big_questions.hint: The chit was red before and after. What is different now?

big_questions.q: If someone knew everything, would they ever say 'might'?
big_questions.hint: Some thinkers say no. Some say that a few things cannot be known by anyone.

big_questions.q: A kea parrot chooses the jar with the better chance. Is the kea doing maths?
big_questions.hint: The kea has no words like will and might. Does thinking about chance need words?

story.title: The Mat by the Door
story.note: Ammu, Unni and Ammachi are made up. The monsoon really does reach Kerala around the start of June most years, and pappadams really are dried in the sun.
text: It was the first week of June in Ammu's village near Alappuzha. Everyone was waiting for the monsoon.
Every morning Ammu ran into the yard and asked the same question. "Ammachi, will it rain today?"
Her grandmother looked at the sky for a long time. Then she always said the same thing. "It might."
"That is not an answer," said Unni. Unni was Ammu's cousin. He was nine, and he liked answers that were short and sure.
On Monday the clouds were grey and low. "It will rain today. Sure," said Unni. He carried his umbrella to school and back. Not one drop fell.
On Tuesday the sky was blue from end to end. "It won't rain today. Sure," said Unni. He left his umbrella at home. At four o'clock a cloud came in from the sea, and he walked home wet to the skin.
Ammachi said nothing. She only moved the umbrella stand a little closer to the door.

That night Ammu lay on her mat and thought. Unni said will, and it did not rain. Unni said won't, and it rained. Ammachi said might on both days, and on both days Ammachi was right. Was 'might' just a trick for never being wrong?
On Wednesday Ammachi had to go to the ration shop. Before she left, she rolled out forty pappadams, round and thin and pale. She gave Ammu a job.
"These must dry in the sun till I come back. A wet pappadam is a spoiled pappadam. Look after them."

Unni looked up. The sky was blue again. "It won't rain," he said. "Put them in the middle of the yard, where the sun is strongest. Then come and play." He had made a paper kite that morning. He left it on the yard wall for the glue to dry, and went down the lane to find string.
Ammu stood with the tray in her hands. She looked at the sky too. Then she tried to sort things, the way she sorted her beads into cups.
"The sun will go down this evening. That is sure. The pappadams won't dry inside the dark kitchen. That is sure too. And the rain?"
She could not put the rain in either cup. It was not a will. It was not a won't. However long she looked at the sky, the rain stayed in the middle.
"So I must be ready for rain, and ready for no rain," she said slowly. "Both at the same time."

She did not carry the tray to the middle of the yard. She dragged Ammachi's big grass mat to the sunny patch right beside the kitchen door. She laid the forty pappadams on it. Then she sat down on the step next to the mat.
Unni came back for his slippers and laughed. "You are guarding pappadams under a blue sky!"
"The sky might change," said Ammu.
"That is not an answer."
"It is the true one," said Ammu.
An hour went by. The pappadams began to curl at the edges. Then the wind turned around. It smelled of wet earth. The coconut leaves started to hiss. One fat drop hit the step.
Ammu took hold of two corners of the mat and pulled. One pull, and forty pappadams slid in through the kitchen door, dry. Then the rain came down so hard that the yard turned white.
Unni came running up the lane with the string in his fist. His kite was still on the wall, in the middle of the rain. When he reached it, it was two sticks and some wet paper.
They sat in the doorway and watched the water pour off the roof.
"How did you know it would rain?" asked Unni.
"I did not know it would rain," said Ammu. "I did not know it wouldn't. That is why the mat was by the door."
Ammachi came home under her umbrella. She counted the pappadams. Forty. She looked at the mat, and at the door, and at Ammu.
"Who told you to put the mat there?"
"Nobody. You say 'might' every day. So I thought about what to do with a might."
The next morning Unni was in the yard first. He looked at the sky for a long time. Then he turned around.
"Ammu," he said, "will it rain today?"
"It might."
Unni nodded, and went in to get his umbrella.
Ammu took her paper boat to the drain by the gate. After yesterday, there was one thing she could say for sure. There would be water in it.
story.epiphany: For the parent: 'might' is not a weak answer or a trick. It is the true answer when a thing can go either way. Ammu sorts what she knows into will, won't and might. Because rain is a 'might', she gets ready for both rain and sun. Unni keeps turning a 'might' into 'will' or 'won't', and is caught out each time.
ask: Unni said 'it will rain' and 'it won't rain'. Why was he wrong both times?
Which things was Ammu sure about? Which thing could she not be sure about?
Why did Ammu put the mat right beside the door?
What is a 'might' in your day tomorrow? How could you be ready for both ways?

experiments.title: The Three Cups Test: will I pick red?
experiments.context: In this test you pick folded paper chits from three cups without looking. One cup has only red chits, one has only blue, and one has both. Before each cup you guess: will I pick red, might I, or won't I? Then you pick many times to find out.
experiments.question: Before you pick, can you tell if the chit will be red? Does it depend on what is in the cup?
experiments.predict: Look at what goes into each cup. Before you pick, say: I will pick red, I might pick red, or I won't pick red. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The chits are all the same size and folded the same way, so your fingers cannot tell them apart. You shut your eyes for every pick. You put the chit back and shake the cup before the next pick, so the cup is the same every time.
results_table: My guess: will, might or won't

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, to tear into 18 small chits
a red crayon and a blue crayon, or sketch pens
steel tumblers or cups you cannot see through
paper and a pencil, for the table

experiments.safety: Keep small things such as chits, coins and beans away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Make 9 red and 9 blue chits. Guess and pick from the red cup, the blue cup and the mixed cup. Try the Closed Hand. Then change a cup.

experiments.record: A grown-up draws the table. For each cup, write the guess first. Then draw a red or blue dot for each pick. At the end, the child says what they found, and the grown-up writes it under the table.

example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like (your guesses and picks will be your own)

setup.art: Eighteen small squares of paper on a floor, nine with a red crayon dot and nine with a blue dot, some already folded in four.
setup.caption: 1. Make 9 red chits and 9 blue chits. Fold each one twice.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers in a row: the first with six red-dot chits beside it, the second with three red and three blue, the third with six blue.
setup.caption: 2. Cup A: 6 red. Cup B: 3 red and 3 blue. Cup C: 6 blue.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut lifting one folded chit out of a steel tumbler, with a paper table and pencil beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Guess. Shut your eyes. Pick one. Open it. Put it back and shake.

flow.do: 1. Tear the paper into 18 pieces, each about as big as a matchbox. 2. Your child draws a big red dot on 9 pieces and a big blue dot on 9. 3. Fold each piece twice, with the dot inside. 4. Check that no colour shows on the outside.
flow.say: We are making chits. Nine get a red dot and nine get a blue dot. Fold each one so the dot hides.
flow.kid: Draw a red dot on 9 papers. Draw a blue dot on 9 papers. Fold each one two times.
flow.context: This is the Three Cups Test, where you pick folded chits from cups without looking. In this first step you make 9 red chits and 9 blue chits.
flow.parent: If the crayon shows through the paper, fold once more or use thicker paper. If you have a carrom board, 9 white and 9 black coins work as well. Then say white for red and black for blue.

flow.do: 1. Let your child watch you put 6 red chits into cup A. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess. 3. Your child shuts their eyes, picks one chit, opens it, and draws a dot in the table. 4. Put the chit back and shake. Do this 6 times.
flow.say: Cup A has six red chits and nothing else. You will pick one without looking. Will it be red, might it be red, or won't it? Why?
flow.kid: Cup A has only red chits. Guess: will you pick red? Now shut your eyes and pick. Do it 6 times.
flow.context: This is the Three Cups Test, where you pick folded chits from cups without looking. In this step you guess and pick from cup A, which has only red chits.

good: There are only red ones.
No blue is in the cup.
It has to be red.

flow.parent: Take any guess that comes with a reason. Do not say who is right. Let the six picks answer.

flow.do: 1. Let your child watch you put 6 blue chits into cup C. 2. Ask for a guess about red, and a reason. Write the guess. 3. Your child picks 6 times with eyes shut, and draws a dot for each pick.
flow.say: Cup C has six blue chits and nothing else. Will you pick red, might you, or won't you? Why?
flow.kid: Cup C has only blue chits. Guess: will you pick red? Shut your eyes and pick 6 times.
flow.context: This is the Three Cups Test, where you pick folded chits from cups without looking. In this step you guess and pick from cup C, which has only blue chits.

ask.q: Could a red chit come out if you tried a hundred times?
good: No. There is no red in the cup.
You cannot pick what is not there.

flow.do: 1. Let your child watch you put 3 red and 3 blue chits into cup B. 2. Ask for a guess about red, and a reason. Write the guess. 3. Before each pick, ask 'Red or blue this time?' 4. Your child picks 10 times with eyes shut, and draws a dot for each pick. Shake the cup each time.
flow.say: Cup B has three red and three blue. Will you pick red, might you, or won't you? Why? Before each pick, tell me the colour you think is coming.
flow.kid: Cup B has red and blue chits. Guess: will you pick red? Pick 10 times. Each time, say the colour first.
flow.context: This is the Three Cups Test, where you pick folded chits from cups without looking. In this step you guess and pick from cup B, which has 3 red and 3 blue chits.

ask.q: Could you tell which colour was coming next?
good: No.
Sometimes I was right and sometimes wrong.
It kept changing.

flow.parent: Most children get red on some picks and blue on others, in a jumbled order. If all ten picks are the same colour, which is very rare, pick ten more.

flow.do: 1. Pick one chit from cup B yourself. 2. Open it so that only you can see, then close your hand over it. 3. Ask your child if the chit is red. 4. Then ask if YOU would say 'might'. 5. Show the chit. Swap places and do it again.
flow.say: I picked a chit and I peeked. Is my chit red: will, might or won't? Now tell me this. Am I unsure too?
flow.kid: Your grown-up picks a chit and peeks. Is it red? Say will, might or won't. Does your grown-up say might too?
flow.context: This is the Closed Hand step of the Three Cups Test. A grown-up picks a chit from the mixed cup, peeks at it, and hides it in a closed hand.

ask.q: It is one chit. Why do you say 'might' when I am sure?
good: You saw it and I did not.
You know. I do not know.
Because you peeked.

flow.parent: Do not explain. The Roots card comes back to this moment. It is enough that your child sees you are sure and they are not.

flow.do: 1. Put 6 blue chits in a cup. 2. Ask your child to change the cup so that red MIGHT come, moving as few chits as they can. 3. Pick 10 times to see. 4. Then ask them to change the cup so that red WILL come. 5. Pick 6 times to check.
flow.say: This cup has six blue chits. Red won't come. Change the cup so that red might come. Move as few chits as you can.
flow.kid: The cup has 6 blue chits. Change it so red might come. Then change it so red will come.
flow.context: This is the Three Cups Test, where you pick folded chits from cups without looking. In this step you change what is in a cup, so that 'won't' turns into 'might', and then into 'will'.

ask.q: What is the smallest change that makes red a 'might'?
good: Put in one red chit.
Swap one blue for one red.

ask.q: What must you do so that red WILL come?
good: Take out all the blue ones.
Only red chits in the cup.

flow.parent: With one red chit among six blue, red may not come in ten picks. That is fine. Tip the cup out and show that the red chit is there. Red still might come.

check.q: A cup has 6 blue chits. You drop in 1 red chit. Now, will you pick red?
check.why: You might. One red chit is in the cup now, so red can come. The six blue chits can come too. Picking 'I won't' usually means that one chit seemed too few to count.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why. 3. Write their words under the table.
flow.say: Look at our three cups. When could you be sure before you picked? When could you not be sure?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which cup was a will? Which was a won't? Which was a might?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Three Cups Test. You say what you found about the red cup, the blue cup and the mixed cup.

ask.q: What do you think now? What did you see? Why is it so?
good: Only red in the cup, so it will be red.
No red in the cup, so it won't be red.
With both colours I could not tell.
It depends on what is in the cup.

check.q: A cup has 2 red chits and 4 blue chits. You pick one without looking. Will it be red?
check.why: It might. Red chits and blue chits are both in the cup, so either colour can come. Picking 'it won't' usually means the blue chits looked like too many. Red is still there.

activities.title: Jump to Your Answer: will, might or won't?
activities.context: In this activity three sheets of paper lie on the floor: Will, Might and Won't. A grown-up says something about today, and you jump to the sheet that fits. It shows that these three words work for your whole day, not only for cups.
activities.problem: Is everything in your day a will, a might or a won't? Try it and see.

schedule.what: Lay out three sheets. Jump to will, might or won't for nine sentences. Then make up your own.

activities.record: Draw three boxes: Will, Might, Won't. Draw one thing from your day in each box.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper on a floor, one step apart, marked with a big tick, a big question mark and a big cross.
setup.caption: 1. Mark three sheets: a tick for Will, a question mark for Might, a cross for Won't.

setup.art: A grown-up reading from a phone while a child stands ready in front of the three sheets.
setup.caption: 2. Listen to the sentence.

setup.art: A child in mid-jump landing on the sheet with the question mark.
setup.caption: 3. Jump to your answer. Say why.

flow.do: 1. Draw a big tick on one sheet, a question mark on the second and a cross on the third. 2. Lay them on the floor, one step apart. 3. Say what each one means.
flow.say: The tick means it will happen. The question mark means it might. The cross means it won't.
flow.kid: Make three sheets: a tick, a question mark and a cross. Put them on the floor.
flow.context: This is Jump to Your Answer, where you sort things in your day into will, might and won't. In this first step you make the three sheets.

flow.do: Read each sentence. Your child jumps to a sheet and says why. 1. The Sun will set this evening. 2. A cow will fly past our window. 3. It will rain today. 4. You will eat something today. 5. Someone will ring our bell today. 6. You will be younger tomorrow than today. 7. A spoon dropped from your hand will fall down. 8. We will see a crow today. 9. Tomorrow will be the day after today.
flow.say: Listen, then jump. The Sun will set this evening. Will, might or won't? Why?
flow.kid: Listen to each sentence. Jump to will, might or won't. Say why.
flow.context: This is Jump to Your Answer, where you sort things in your day into will, might and won't. In this step you jump to a sheet for nine sentences about today.

ask.q: Why is 'someone will ring our bell' a might?
good: Someone can come, or nobody comes.
We do not know yet.

flow.parent: Will: 1, 4, 7 and 9. Won't: 2 and 6. Might: 3, 5 and 8. If your child gives a good reason for another answer, accept it. In a city full of crows, sentence 8 is close to a will.

flow.do: 1. Go back to 'It will rain today'. 2. Ask what the answer would be in the rainiest month where you live, and in the driest. 3. Your child makes up three sentences for you, one for each sheet. You jump.
flow.say: Think of the rainiest month here. What would you say about rain then? Now make up three sentences for me to jump to.
flow.kid: Make up one will, one might and one won't. Your grown-up jumps this time.
flow.context: This is Jump to Your Answer, where you sort things in your day into will, might and won't. In this last step you make up your own sentences, and a grown-up jumps.

ask.q: Can the same sentence be a might in one place and nearly a will in another?
good: Yes. Rain in the monsoon is nearly sure.
It depends where you are and when.

check.q: Which of these will happen for sure?
check.why: Night comes after every day, so that is a will. Rain and a visit can happen or not happen, so they are both 'might'.

activities.title: Maths in sport: the cricket toss
activities.context: In this activity you toss a coin the way two cricket captains do before a match. The captain who wins the toss chooses to bat or to bowl first. You will use a toss for a real choice at home, and find out if anyone can tell how a coin will land.
activities.problem: Two captains both want to choose. Why do they let a coin decide?

materials.item: a coin, such as a 5 rupee coin
a towel or a bed to toss onto, so the coin does not roll away

activities.safety: Keep small things such as chits, coins and beans away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Toss for a real choice. Then call ten tosses and mark how many calls were right.

activities.record: Draw ten boxes in a row. For each toss, draw a tick if your call was right and a cross if it was wrong.

setup.art: Close view of the two sides of an Indian coin: the side with the lions, labelled heads, and the side with the number, labelled tails.
setup.caption: 1. Find heads, the side with the lions. The other side is tails.

setup.art: A grown-up flipping a coin into the air above a folded towel while a child calls out with a hand raised.
setup.caption: 2. One tosses. The other calls 'heads' or 'tails' while the coin is in the air.

setup.art: A strip of ten hand-drawn boxes on paper, the first four filled with ticks and crosses.
setup.caption: 3. Tick if the call was right. Cross if it was wrong.

flow.do: 1. Look at both sides of the coin. The side with the lions is heads. The side with the number is tails. 2. Choose something real to decide, such as who picks tonight's story. 3. You toss. Your child calls while the coin is in the air. 4. Keep to what the coin says.
flow.say: Cricket captains toss a coin to see who chooses first. We will toss for who picks tonight's story. Call heads or tails!
flow.kid: Find heads and tails on the coin. When the coin is in the air, call one. Did you win the toss?
flow.context: This is the Cricket Toss, where a coin is tossed to choose who goes first. In this first step you toss once for a real choice at home.
flow.parent: Keeping to the result matters. It shows your child that both sides accept a toss because neither can tell how it will land.

flow.do: 1. Draw ten boxes in a row. 2. Toss ten times. Your child calls each time before the coin lands. 3. Draw a tick for a right call and a cross for a wrong one. 4. Count the ticks.
flow.say: Now call ten tosses. Try as hard as you can to get every one right.
flow.kid: Call ten tosses. Tick the box when you are right. How many ticks?
flow.context: This is the Cricket Toss, where a coin is tossed to choose who goes first. In this step you call ten tosses and mark each call right or wrong.

ask.q: Did you find a way to get every call right?
good: No.
I got some right and some wrong.
You cannot tell.

flow.parent: Most children get between 3 and 7 right out of ten. Getting all ten right by luck is very rare.

flow.do: 1. Ask the three questions below. 2. Ask why captains use a coin and do not just talk it over.
flow.say: Before a toss: will the coin show heads? Will it show heads or tails? Will it show a 6?
flow.kid: Will the coin show heads? Will it show heads or tails? Will it show a 6?
flow.context: This is the Cricket Toss, where a coin is tossed to choose who goes first. In this last step you use will, might and won't for a coin.

ask.q: Why do both captains trust the coin?
good: Nobody can tell how it lands.
It does not take sides.
Both have the same chance.

flow.parent: Heads is a might. Heads or tails is a will. A 6 is a won't. A coin can land on its edge, but that is so rare on a towel that we leave it out.

check.q: You toss a coin once. Which of these will happen for sure?
check.why: A coin has only two sides, so one of the two must show. Heads alone is a might. Tails alone is a might too.

activities.title: Dice Talk: what can a dice show?
activities.context: In this activity you look at every face of a dice and draw all six. Then you use your drawing to say what you will roll, what you might roll and what you won't. It shows how to find the answer by looking at everything that can come up.
activities.problem: To say will, might or won't about a dice, first find out everything the dice can show.
activities.safety: Keep small things such as chits, coins and beans away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Draw the six faces of a dice. Say will, might or won't for six sentences. Then roll 12 times and mark what came.

activities.record: Draw the six faces in a row. Under each face, make one mark every time that face comes up in 12 rolls.

setup.art: A child turning a dice over in her fingers and looking closely at one face.
setup.caption: 1. Turn the dice. Find every face.

setup.art: Six squares drawn in a row on paper, showing one to six dots.
setup.caption: 2. Draw all six faces in a row.

setup.art: A dice showing 4 on a floor, and a pencil making a mark under the drawn face with four dots.
setup.caption: 3. Roll 12 times. Make a mark under the face that comes up.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the dice. 2. Ask them to find every face and count the dots on each. 3. They draw the six faces in a row.
flow.say: Turn the dice around. How many faces does it have? What is on each face?
flow.kid: Look at every face of the dice. Count the dots. Draw all six faces.
flow.context: This is Dice Talk, where you find everything a dice can show. In this first step you draw all six faces of the dice.

ask.q: Is there a face with 7 dots? Is there a face with no dots?
good: No. It goes from 1 to 6.
The biggest is 6 and the smallest is 1.

chart.title: The six faces of a dice

flow.do: Say each sentence. Your child looks at their drawing and says will, might or won't. 1. I will roll a 4. 2. I will roll a 7. 3. I will roll a number smaller than 7. 4. I will roll a 1 or a 2. 5. I will roll a 0. 6. I will roll 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.
flow.say: Look at your six faces. I say: I will roll a 7. Will I, might I, or won't I? How do you know?
flow.kid: Look at your drawing. Your grown-up says a sentence. Say will, might or won't.
flow.context: This is Dice Talk, where you find everything a dice can show. In this step you use your drawing of the six faces to say will, might or won't.
flow.parent: Might: 1 and 4. Won't: 2 and 5. Will: 3 and 6. Ask 'Which faces make it true?' and let your child point at them.

check.q: You roll one dice. Will you get a number smaller than 7?
check.why: You will. The faces are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, and every one of them is smaller than 7. Picking 'I might' usually means thinking of one face and not all six.

flow.do: 1. Ask: if we roll 12 times, will every face come up at least once? Take a guess and a reason. 2. Roll 12 times. Your child makes a mark under the face that comes up. 3. Look at which faces came often and which did not come.
flow.say: We will roll 12 times. Will every face come up? Will, might or won't? Why?
flow.kid: Roll 12 times. Make a mark under the face that comes. Did every face come?
flow.context: This is Dice Talk, where you find everything a dice can show. In this last step you roll 12 times and mark which faces came up.

ask.q: One face did not come at all. Does that mean it won't ever come?
good: No. It is on the dice.
It still might come next time.

flow.parent: It is a might. In 12 rolls, at least one face is usually missing. A missing face is still a might, because it is on the dice.

games.title: Call It!
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a card game played with one dice. Each card says something about the next roll, such as 'You will roll a 7'. You call will, might or won't, then turn the card over to check. It builds quick use of the three words.

printables.title: 12 Call It cards. The sentence is on the front and the answer is on the back.

items.b: Won't. A dice goes only from 1 to 6.

items.f: You will roll a number smaller than 7.
items.b: Will. Every face is smaller than 7.
Might. One face shows 3. Five faces do not.
Won't. No face has zero dots.
Will. Those are all the faces.

items.f: You will roll a number bigger than 2.
items.b: Might. 3, 4, 5 and 6 are bigger. 1 and 2 are not.

items.f: You will roll a number bigger than 6.
You will roll a number bigger than 0.
items.b: Will. Every face is bigger than 0.

items.f: You will roll a 4 or a 5.
items.b: Might. Two faces fit. Four faces do not.

rules: Shuffle the 12 cards. Put them in a pile with the sentences facing up. Put a heap of beans beside the pile.
On your turn, read the top card aloud, or ask a grown-up to read it. Call 'will', 'might' or 'won't'.
Turn the card over to check. If your call was right, keep the card. If not, slide it under the pile.
Then roll the dice once. If what the card said came true on your roll, take one bean.
The game ends when the pile is gone. Count one for each card and one for each bean. The biggest count wins.
Playing alone: count how many of the 12 cards you call right the first time. Play again and try to beat that.

setup.art: A small pile of paper cards with a sentence on the top card, a dice and a heap of beans on a floor.
setup.caption: 1. Pile the cards with the sentences up. Put the dice and beans near.

setup.art: A child holding a card that reads 'You will roll a 7' and saying 'Won't!'
setup.caption: 2. Read the card. Call will, might or won't.

setup.art: The card turned over showing its answer, a dice showing 3 beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card to check. Then roll once.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards, or copy them on slips of paper with the answer on the back. 2. Shuffle them. Pile them with the sentences up. 3. Put the dice and the beans beside the pile.
flow.say: Each card says something about the next roll. You call will, might or won't.
flow.kid: Pile the cards with the sentences up. Put the dice and the beans near.
flow.context: This is Call It, a card game about what a dice will, might and won't show. In this first step you set out the cards, the dice and the beans.

chart.title: The six faces of a dice

flow.do: 1. Take one practice turn each. 2. Read the top card. Call. Turn it over to check. 3. Roll once and see if the card came true.
flow.say: My card says: you will roll a 3. I call 'might'. Now I check, and then I roll.
flow.kid: Read the top card. Call will, might or won't. Turn it over. Then roll.
flow.context: This is Call It, a card game about what a dice will, might and won't show. In this step each player takes one practice turn.

check.q: A card says 'You will roll a 3'. You roll a 5. Was 'might' the right call?
check.why: Yes. 'Might' means it can happen and it can also not happen. This time it did not happen. The call was still right.

flow.parent: A 'might' card sometimes comes true and sometimes does not. A 'will' card comes true on every roll, and a 'won't' card never does. Let your child notice this.

flow.do: 1. Play until the pile is gone. 2. Now and then ask which faces would make the card come true.
flow.say: Which faces make this card come true? Point to them on the dice.
flow.kid: Play the game. Keep each card you call right. Take a bean when a card comes true.
flow.context: This is Call It, a card game about what a dice will, might and won't show. In this step you play until the pile of cards is gone.

ask.q: Which kind of card gives you a bean every time?
good: The will cards.
The ones that are sure.

flow.do: 1. Each player counts their cards and beans. 2. Sort all 12 cards into three heaps by their answers: will, might, won't.
flow.say: Count your cards and beans. Now let us put all the cards into three heaps.
flow.kid: Count your cards and beans. Then sort the cards: will, might, won't.
flow.context: This is Call It, a card game about what a dice will, might and won't show. In this last step you count up and sort the cards into three heaps.

games.title: Red Road, Blue Road
games.players: 1 or 2 players: alone or with a parent or friend
games.context: This is a race game for two counters on two short roads. A chit picked from a cup says which counter moves. One player fills the cup, and the other calls if Red will win, might win or won't win. It shows that what is in the cup decides the race.

printables.title: Two roads side by side, each with a Start square, 4 squares and a Home square

rules: You need the red and blue chits from the Three Cups Test, one cup, two buttons and some beans.
One player owns the Red road. The other owns the Blue road. Put a button on each Start.
Take turns to be the cup maker. The cup maker puts any 6 chits in the cup and shows them.
The other player is the caller. The caller looks and calls: 'Red will win', 'Red might win' or 'Red won't win'.
Now race. Pick a chit without looking. Red chit: the Red button moves one square. Blue chit: the Blue button moves one. Put the chit back and shake.
The first button to reach Home wins the race. Its owner takes a bean. The caller takes a bean if the call was right. 'Might' is right if the cup had both colours.
Play 4 races. The player with the most beans wins.
Playing alone: put 3 red and 3 blue in the cup. Guess which road wins. Race. Then try 5 red and 1 blue.

setup.art: Two paper tracks side by side, one coloured red and one blue, each with six squares, a button on each Start.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the two roads side by side. Put a button on each Start.

setup.art: A child putting six chits into a steel tumbler while another player watches closely.
setup.caption: 2. The cup maker shows 6 chits and puts them in. The caller calls.

setup.art: An opened red chit beside the tumbler and a finger pushing the button on the red road one square forward.
setup.caption: 3. Pick a chit. Move that colour one square. Put the chit back.

flow.do: 1. Draw two roads of 6 squares each, side by side. Colour one red and one blue. 2. Put a button on each Start. 3. Choose who owns Red and who owns Blue.
flow.say: This is a race between Red and Blue. The chits decide who moves.
flow.kid: Draw two roads with 6 squares each. Put a button on each Start.
flow.context: This is Red Road, Blue Road, a race game where chits picked from a cup move two counters. In this first step you draw the two roads.

flow.do: 1. For a practice race, put 3 red and 3 blue chits in the cup. 2. Ask your child to call. 3. Race: pick, move, put back, shake.
flow.say: Three red and three blue are in the cup. Will Red win, might Red win, or won't Red win?
flow.kid: The cup has 3 red and 3 blue. Call it. Then pick chits and race.
flow.context: This is Red Road, Blue Road, a race game where chits picked from a cup move two counters. In this step you play a practice race with 3 red and 3 blue chits in the cup.

check.q: The cup has 6 red chits and no blue. Which road wins the race?
check.why: Red will win. Every chit is red, so only the Red button ever moves. Blue stays on Start.

flow.do: 1. Play 4 races. Swap the cup maker each time. 2. Let your child find out what happens when the cup maker uses only their own colour.
flow.say: You are the cup maker now. Put in any six chits you like, and show me.
flow.kid: Play 4 races. Take turns to fill the cup. Call before each race.
flow.context: This is Red Road, Blue Road, a race game where chits picked from a cup move two counters. In this step you play 4 races and take turns to fill the cup.

ask.q: You put in only red. Was that race fair to Blue?
good: No. Blue could not move.
Blue had no chance.

flow.parent: Sooner or later one of you fills the cup with one colour. Enjoy it. Then ask what cup would give both roads a chance.

flow.do: 1. Count the beans. 2. Ask which cup made the most exciting race.
flow.say: Count your beans. Which cup gave the best race? Why?
flow.kid: Count your beans. Which cup made the best race?
flow.context: This is Red Road, Blue Road, a race game where chits picked from a cup move two counters. In this last step you count the beans and talk about the best race.

projects.title: Sky Watch: will it rain today?
projects.context: In this five-day project you look at the sky each morning and say if it will rain, might rain or won't rain. Each evening you mark what really happened. It shows how 'might' works for the weather where you live.
projects.problem: Can anyone say for sure in the morning what the sky will do by evening?

materials.item: a sheet of paper for the table, and a pencil
a window, balcony or doorstep where you can see the sky

schedule.what: Draw the table. Look at the morning sky and write will, might or won't. In the evening, mark rain or no rain.
Morning: look and call. Evening: mark what happened.
Morning: look and call. Evening: mark what happened.
Morning: look and call. Evening: mark what happened.
Morning: look and call. Evening: mark what happened. Then count your calls.

projects.record: A table with three columns: the day, my morning call, and what happened by evening. Draw a small cloud with drops for rain and a small Sun for no rain.

setup.art: A hand-drawn table on paper with three columns and five empty rows, taped beside a window.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with 5 rows: day, my call, what happened.

setup.art: A child at a window in the morning looking up at clouds, pencil in hand.
setup.caption: 2. Each morning, look at the sky. Write will, might or won't.

setup.art: The same child in the evening drawing a small rain cloud in the last column.
setup.caption: 3. Each evening, draw rain or Sun.

flow.do: 1. Draw the table with your child and tape it near a window. 2. In the morning, look at the sky together. 3. Your child says if it will rain, might rain or won't rain today, and why. Write it. 4. In the evening, your child draws rain or Sun.
flow.say: Look at the sky. Will it rain today, might it, or won't it? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the sky. Will it rain today? Write will, might or won't. Check in the evening.
flow.context: This is Sky Watch, a five-day project about rain. On day 1 you draw the table, make your first call and check it in the evening.

flow.do: 1. On days 2, 3 and 4, do the same. Morning: look and call. Evening: mark. 2. If you like, read out today's forecast from a newspaper or a weather app, and listen for words like 'likely'.
flow.say: What does the sky say this morning? What clues are you using?
flow.kid: Each morning, look at the sky and call. Each evening, draw rain or Sun.
flow.context: This is Sky Watch, a five-day project about rain. On days 2 to 4 you call the rain each morning and check each evening.

ask.q: What clues in the sky help you call?
good: Dark clouds.
Wind.
It rained yesterday.
The sky is all blue.

flow.wait: Do this on each of the next three days.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, call and mark as before. 2. Then count together: on how many 'might' days did it rain? On how many did it stay dry? 3. Ask if any 'will' or 'won't' call turned out wrong.
flow.say: Count your 'might' days. On how many did it rain? Did a 'will' or a 'won't' ever go wrong?
flow.kid: Count your might days. How many had rain? How many had no rain?
flow.context: This is Sky Watch, a five-day project about rain. On day 5 you count how your morning calls turned out.

ask.q: Is 'might' a lazy answer for rain, or the true one?
good: The true one. You cannot tell in the morning.
Sometimes it rained and sometimes not.

flow.parent: In a dry month, most calls will be 'won't' and that is fine. Run the project again when the season changes, and compare the two tables.

challenges.title: Stretch: the Almost-Sure Cup
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 1. You build a cup of 6 chits in which red comes most of the time, but blue still might come. It shows that one 'might' can be bigger than another.
challenges.problem: Build a cup of 6 chits. Red must come much more often than blue. But blue must still be a 'might', not a 'won't'.
constraints: The cup must hold exactly 6 chits.
Blue must be able to come out.
You test the cup with 12 picks, putting the chit back each time.
materials: the red and blue chits from the Three Cups Test
general: Put in 4 red chits and 2 blue chits.
Put in 5 red chits and 1 blue chit.
creative: Build two cups, one with 4 red and one with 5 red. Test both and see which gives more red.
Build the opposite cup, where red hardly ever comes, and test that too.
challenges.your_turn: Now choose your own 6 chits. Test your cup with 12 picks. If red did not come much more often than blue, change the cup and test again.

setup.art: Six empty outlines of chits beside a steel tumbler, with heaps of red and blue chits to choose from.
setup.caption: 1. Choose 6 chits for your cup.

setup.art: A child picking a chit with eyes shut, and a paper with a row of red and blue dots growing beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Pick 12 times. Draw a dot for each pick.

setup.art: Two rows of twelve dots on paper, the first mostly red, the second half red and half blue.
setup.caption: 3. Count the red dots and the blue dots.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Let your child choose 6 chits and say why. 3. Do not correct the choice.
flow.say: Build a cup of six chits where red comes most of the time. But blue must still be a might.
flow.kid: Choose 6 chits. Red must come most of the time. Blue must still be a might.
flow.context: This is the Almost-Sure Cup challenge, where you build a cup in which red comes much more often than blue. In this first step you choose 6 chits for your cup.

ask.q: Why did you choose those six?
good: More red means red comes more.
One blue so that blue can still come.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks 12 times with eyes shut. Put the chit back and shake each time. 2. Draw a red or blue dot for each pick. 3. Count the red dots and the blue dots.
flow.say: Pick twelve times. Draw a dot each time. Then count each colour.
flow.kid: Pick 12 times. Draw a dot for each pick. Count the red and the blue.
flow.context: This is the Almost-Sure Cup challenge, where you build a cup in which red comes much more often than blue. In this step you test your cup with 12 picks.
flow.parent: With 5 red and 1 blue, about 10 of the 12 picks are red. Now and then blue does not come at all in 12 picks. Then tip out the cup and show that blue is there. It still might come.

flow.do: 1. Put 3 red and 3 blue in a second cup. Pick 12 times and draw the dots under the first row. 2. Compare the two rows. 3. Give the words: in the first cup red is likely and blue is unlikely.
flow.say: Look at the two rows. In which cup did red come more often? Why?
flow.kid: Test a cup with 3 red and 3 blue. Which cup gave more red?
flow.context: This is the Almost-Sure Cup challenge, where you build a cup in which red comes much more often than blue. In this step you compare your cup with a cup of 3 red and 3 blue chits.

ask.q: Both cups are a 'might' for red. What is different?
good: One has more red in it.
Red comes more often from the first cup.

check.q: Cup P has 5 red and 1 blue. Cup Q has 1 red and 5 blue. From which cup is red more likely?
check.why: Cup P. It holds many more red chits, so red comes more often. Red is a 'might' in both cups, but the two mights are not the same size.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to explain their cup to someone else at home. 2. Ask what cup they would build if blue should come most of the time.
flow.say: Tell me how your cup works. How would you make blue the likely one?
flow.kid: Tell someone how your cup works. How would you make blue come most?
flow.context: This is the Almost-Sure Cup challenge, where you build a cup in which red comes much more often than blue. In this last step you explain how your cup works.

items.p: Every chit in this cup is red. You pick one without looking. Will it be red?
items.why: It will. Every chit in the cup is red, so no other colour can come out.

items.p: This cup has only blue chits. You pick one without looking. You won't pick red.
items.why: True. There is no red chit in the cup. You cannot pick what is not there.

items.p: Look at this cup. You pick one chit with your eyes shut. Will it be red?
items.why: It might. The cup has red chits and blue chits, so either colour can come out.

items.p: The Sun will set this evening.
items.why: True. The Earth keeps turning, so the Sun sets every evening. This is a will.

items.p: Sort these six things: will, might or won't?
items: A cow flies past the window
You roll a 4 on a dice
You roll a 9 on a dice
items.why:
The Sun rises every day, and dropped things fall, so those two are will.
Rain and a 4 on a dice can happen or not, so they are might.
Cows cannot fly and a dice has no 9, so those two are won't.

items.p: Count the faces of a dice. A dice has ____ faces.
items.why: A dice has 6 faces. They show 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 dots.

items.p: You roll one dice. Which of these will you get for sure?
items.why: A dice shows only 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. So a number from 1 to 6 is sure. A 6 is only a might. A 7 is a won't.

items.p: Every part of this spinner is shaded. Will it stop on a shaded part?
items.why: It will. There is no white part to stop on.

items.p: No part of this spinner is shaded. It might stop on a shaded part.
items.why: False. There is no shaded part to stop on. So this is a won't, not a might.

items.p: This cup has 3 red and 3 blue chits. You can tell which colour will come next.
items.why: False. Both colours are in the cup, so either can come. Nobody can tell before the pick.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: Will is for sure things. Won't is for things that cannot happen. Might is for everything in between.

items.p: Draw a cup of chits from which you won't pick blue.
items.a: Any cup with no blue chit in it, such as a cup of only red chits.
items.why: If no blue chit is in the cup, blue cannot come out.

items.p: Draw a spinner that will stop on red for sure.
items.a: A circle with every part coloured red.
items.why: If every part is red, the spinner has nowhere else to stop.

items.p: Say it aloud. Cup A had only red chits. Why did you pick red every time?
items.a: Because every chit in cup A was red. There was nothing else to pick.
items.why: A strong answer looks at everything in the cup. All of it was red, so red was sure.

items.p: This cup has 1 red chit and 5 blue. You pick one without looking. Will it be red?
items.why: It might. One red chit is in the cup, so red can come. Picking 'it won't' usually means that one chit seemed too few to count.

items.p: This cup has 5 red chits and 1 blue. You pick one without looking. Will it be red?
items.why: It might. Most chits are red, but one is blue, and blue can come. Picking 'it will' forgets the blue chit.

items.p: A cup has 6 blue chits. You add 1 red chit. Now red is a 'might'.
items.why: True. Before, red was a won't. One red chit is enough to turn it into a might.

items.p: This cup has 3 red and 3 blue. To make red a 'will', take out ____ blue chits.
items.why: Take out all 3 blue chits. Then only red chits are left, so nothing else can come out.

items.p: From a mixed cup you picked blue 3 times, putting it back each time. So the next pick will be red.
items.why: False. The cup is just the same on every pick. The next chit might be red, and it might be blue again.

items.p: You toss a coin once. Sort each one: will, might or won't?
items.why:
Heads alone and tails alone are each a might.
One of the two must show, and the coin must come down, so those are will.
A coin has no 5, so that is a won't.

items.p: One part of this spinner is shaded. Will it stop on the shaded part?
items.why: It might. It can stop on the shaded part or on a white part.

items.p: This cup has 4 red chits. To make blue a 'might', add at least ____ blue chit.
items.why: One blue chit is enough. Then blue can come out.

items.p: Picking red: put the cups in order, from won't, to might, to will.
items.why:
With 6 blue, red won't come.
With both colours, red might come.
With 6 red, red will come.

items.p: Amma peeks at the chit in her hand. You do not. Who says 'it might be red'?
items.why: Only you. Amma has seen the chit, so she is sure. You have not seen it, so for you it is a might.

items.p: Draw a spinner with 4 parts that might stop on red.
items.a: A circle cut into 4 parts with 1, 2 or 3 parts coloured red.
items.why: For a might, some parts must be red and some must not be red.

items.p: Name one thing that will happen today, one that might, and one that won't.
items.a: For example: night will come, a friend might visit, I won't grow wings.
items.why: A strong answer has a sure thing, a thing that can go either way, and a thing that cannot happen.

items.p: The morning sky is clear and blue. Will it rain today?

views.says: It won't rain. There is not one cloud.
It might. Clouds can come by evening.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For example: it might rain, because the morning sky does not show the whole day. Meenakshi is right that a clear sky makes rain less likely.
items.why: A clear morning is a clue, but it does not make rain impossible. For most days 'might' is the honest call.

items.p: You roll one dice. Will you get a number bigger than 3?
items.why: You might. The faces 4, 5 and 6 are bigger than 3. The faces 1, 2 and 3 are not.

chart.title: The six faces of a dice

items.p: This goes past Class 1. From which cup is red more likely?
items.why: Cup P. It has 5 red chits and cup Q has only 1. Red is a might in both cups, but it comes more often from cup P.

items.p: If a thing has never happened before, it won't ever happen.
items.why: False. 'I have never seen it' is not the same as 'it cannot happen'. People in Europe had seen only white swans, until sailors saw black swans in Australia.

items.p: Which change makes red a 'will'?
opts: Take out all the blue chits
items.why: Take out all the blue chits. Then only red is left. Adding one red still leaves blue in the cup. Shaking changes nothing.

items.p: Which change makes red a 'won't'?
opts: Swap every red chit for a blue one
items.why: Swap every red chit for a blue one. Then no red is in the cup. Adding one blue makes red a might, not a won't.

items.p: A spinner has 4 parts, all shaded. For it to 'might stop on white', make at least ____ part white.
items.why: One white part is enough. Then the spinner can stop on white.

items.p: Sort these six: will, might or won't?
items: Ice left in the hot sun melts
You grow taller than a coconut tree by tomorrow
items.why:
The order of the days and ice melting in the sun are sure.
A toss and a visit can go either way.
Nobody grows that much in a day, and a dice has no 0.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. 'Might' always means it happens half the time.
items.why: False. One red chit among six is a might. Five red chits among six is also a might. Red comes far more often from the second cup.

items.p: A cup has 1 red and 5 blue. In 10 picks, red never came. So red won't ever come.
items.why: False. The red chit is still in the cup, so red can come on the next pick. 'Might' never promised that red would come in ten picks.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. Put the cups in order, from red least likely to red most likely.
items.why:
Each cup has 6 chits.
The more of them are red, the more often red comes.

items.p: A cup has 6 chits. You will pick red for sure. So ____ of the chits are red.
items.why: All 6. If even one chit were blue, blue might come, and red would not be sure.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. Draw a cup of 6 chits where red comes most, but blue still might.
items.a: A cup with 4 or 5 red chits and the rest blue.
items.why: Blue must be in the cup to be a might. Red must be the bigger group to come most often.

items.p: Say a 'might' sentence about tomorrow. Then change one thing to make it a 'will'.
items.a: For example: 'I might see Paatti tomorrow.' If we go to her house, 'I will see Paatti tomorrow.'
items.why: A strong answer shows that a might turns into a will when the other way is taken away.

items.p: Two thinkers argue about the word 'might'.

views.says: If we knew everything, we would never need to say might.
Some things nobody can know before they happen.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other thinker has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason from the unit. For example: the one who peeked at the chit was sure. Or: nobody can tell how a coin will land.
items.why: This is a real argument with no agreed answer. Mathematicians and physicists have held both views.

quiz.p: This cup has 4 chits. You pick one with your eyes shut. Will it be red?
quiz.why: It will. All four chits are red, so only red can come out.

quiz.p: You roll one dice. Will you roll an 8?
quiz.why: You won't. A dice shows only 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

quiz.p: This cup has 4 red chits and 2 blue. Will you pick red?
quiz.why: You might. Red and blue are both in the cup, so either can come out. Picking 'I will' forgets the blue chits.

quiz.p: How do you find out if you will, might or won't pick red?
opts: Look at all the chits in the cup
quiz.why: Look at everything that can come out. All red means will. No red means won't. Some red means might.

quiz.p: A cup has red and blue chits. Before you pick, you can know the colour you will get.
quiz.why: False. With both colours in the cup, nobody can tell which one comes this time.

quiz.p: A coin landed tails 2 times. What about the next toss?
opts: It might be heads or tails
quiz.why: It might be heads or tails. The coin is just the same on every toss. Picking 'it will be heads' means thinking heads is waiting for a turn.

quiz.p: A cup has 5 blue chits. Which change makes red a 'might'?
quiz.why: Add 1 red chit. Then red is in the cup and can come out. More blue or more shaking puts no red in the cup.

quiz.p: This cup has 2 red and 2 blue. Which change makes red a 'will'?
quiz.why: Take out the 2 blue chits. Then only red is left. Adding a red chit still leaves blue in the cup.

quiz.p: Sort these four: will, might or won't?
items: The Moon falls into your garden
quiz.why:
Night and eating come every day, so they are will.
Rain can come or not, so it is might.
The Moon stays far away in the sky, so that is won't.

quiz.p: The weather report says 'rain is likely today'. Which word fits best?
quiz.why: Might. 'Likely' means rain can well come, but it is not sure. So you carry an umbrella and hope for the best.

quiz.p: Paatti hides a chit in her hand. She has seen it. You have not. Who is sure of its colour?
quiz.why: Only Paatti. She has seen the chit. For you it is still a might.

quiz.p: The same chit can be a 'might' for one person and 'sure' for another.
quiz.why: True. It depends on what each person knows. The one who peeked is sure. The one who did not peek says might.

open_questions.q: Is anything in the world a real 'might', or do we say might only because we do not know enough?
open_questions.why_open: Thinkers have argued about this for hundreds of years. Many physicists say some tiny happenings cannot be known ahead by anyone. Others are not so sure.

open_questions.q: How do kea and other animals use chance in their daily lives?

open_questions.q: Can tomorrow's rain ever be told for sure?
open_questions.why_open: Weather reports get better every year. But the air is always moving, and tiny changes can grow into big ones. Nobody knows how far ahead a sure report can ever reach.

maths.problem: A cup has 4 red chits and 2 blue chits. How many chits are in the cup? Will you pick red for sure?
maths.answer: 6 chits. No, red is a might.
maths.explain: Count on from 4: 5, 6. There are 6 chits. Two of them are blue, so blue can come. Red is a might, not a will.
maths.context: In the Three Cups Test you looked at what was in a cup before you picked. Here you count the chits first.
maths.why_maths: Counting everything that can come out is the first step in saying will, might or won't.

maths.problem: Kavya called 10 coin tosses. She was right 6 times. How many times was she wrong?
maths.explain: Ten tosses in all, and 6 calls were right. 10 take away 6 is 4. So 4 calls were wrong. Even a careful caller gets some wrong, because each toss is a might.
maths.context: In the Cricket Toss you called ten tosses and ticked the ones you got right. This uses the same count.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells you how many calls went wrong without counting the crosses.

maths.problem: Cup P has 5 red chits and 1 blue. Cup Q has 2 red chits and 4 blue. Which cup has more red chits? From which cup does red come more often?
maths.explain: 5 is more than 2, so cup P has more red chits. Both cups hold 6 chits. The cup with more red in it gives red more often.
maths.context: In the Almost-Sure Cup challenge you built a cup where red came most of the time. Here you compare two cups.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two numbers tells you which 'might' is the bigger one.

maths.problem: A cup has 6 chits. Lakshmi says, 'I will pick red for sure.' She is right. How many of the chits are red? How many are blue?
maths.explain: If even one chit were blue, blue might come, and red would not be sure. So every chit is red. That makes 6 red and no blue.
maths.context: In the Three Cups Test, red was sure only from the cup with nothing but red chits. This puzzle works backwards from that.
maths.why_maths: Thinking backwards from 'sure' tells you what must be in the cup without looking.

maths.problem: Farhan rolled a dice 12 times. The table shows how many times each face came. Which face did not come? Does that mean it won't ever come?
maths.answer: The face 3 did not come. No, it still might.
maths.explain: The table shows 0 for the face 3. But 3 is on the dice, so it can come on the next roll. 'It has not come yet' is not the same as 'it won't come'.
maths.context: In Dice Talk you rolled a dice 12 times and marked each face that came up. Here is another child's table.
maths.why_maths: A table of marks shows at a glance what came often and what did not come.

roots.context: We picked chits from cups and said will, might and won't. Now let us think about what 'might' really tells us.

deep_truth.truth: In the Three Cups Test, a grown-up picked a chit, peeked, and closed their hand. For you, the chit might be red. For the grown-up it was sure, because they had seen it. It was the same chit at the same time. So 'might' also tells what a person knows.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'might' is inside the thing, like its colour. But the chit in the hand was already red or blue. Only your knowing was missing.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Closed Hand step of the Three Cups Test, one chit was a 'might' for you and sure for the one who peeked.

three.who_am_i: You do not know what tomorrow will bring. You still pack your bag and take your umbrella. You live with 'might' every day.
three.what_is_life: Other living beings meet 'might' too. In a test, kea parrots chose the hand that had the better chance of holding a treat.
three.what_is_this_world: A few things in the world are sure, like the Sun rising. Many more are a 'might', like rain.

roots.thread: Before the hand opens, the chit could be red or it could be blue. Many things might be. Then the hand opens, and there is one colour. Every moment is like this. Out of all that might happen, one thing does happen.

teachings.teaching: This old hymn asks where the world came from. It ends by saying that the one who watches from the highest sky knows. Or maybe even he does not know.
teachings.link: The hymn does not pretend to be sure. It ends on a 'might'. Saying 'might' when you do not know is the honest answer.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching, an old Chinese book, says: to know that you do not know is best.
teachings.link: In the Closed Hand step you had not seen the chit. You said 'it might be red'. You knew that you did not know.

teachings.teaching: In this hymn, a man has lost everything by playing dice. He is told: do not play with dice. Plough your field.
teachings.link: About three thousand years ago, people already knew that nobody can tell how dice will fall. A dice is a 'might' that no wishing can turn into a 'will'.

science.text: In a test in 2020, six kea parrots mostly chose the closed hand that came from the jar with more treat tokens. They could not see the token in the hand. They used what they knew about the jar (Bastos and Taylor, 2020).
Is anything in the world a real 'might', even for someone who knows everything? Many physicists say yes. The question is still argued about.

other_view.view: They say some 'mights' are real, and have nothing to do with what a person knows. Take one tiny atom of the metal uranium. It can break apart at any moment. They say nobody could tell when, even someone who knew everything. If that is so, 'might' is in the world itself.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that chance can be thought about carefully? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years people played with dice. Most of them thought that nothing could be worked out about dice. They said it was all luck. A hymn in the Rig Veda, about 3,000 years old, tells of a man who lost everything at dice. Around 1565 an Italian doctor, Gerolamo Cardano, wrote a small book about dice games. He began by listing everything the dice can show, and counted. His book was printed only in 1663, long after he died. In 1654 two French mathematicians, Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat, wrote letters to each other about a game that stops halfway. How should the players share the prize? They found a fair way by listing every way the game could go on. So a 'might' can be studied. The first step is the one you took with the cups: look at everything that can come out.
how_we_found_out.who: Gerolamo Cardano, and later Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Nothing can be worked out about dice, because it is all luck. Cardano, Pascal and Fermat showed this was wrong. They listed everything that could happen, counted, and got answers that others could check.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Three Cups Test needs 18 chits, which take about 4 minutes to make with a child. Cup A gives red every time and cup C never does. Cup B gives a jumbled mix. If all ten picks from cup B are one colour, which is very rare, the step says to pick ten more. With one red chit among six blue, red often does not come in ten picks, so the step says to tip the cup out and show the red chit. Thin paper can let the crayon show through, so the step says to fold once more or use carrom coins. Call It was played in the head with 1 and 2 players: 12 cards (3 will, 4 won't, 5 might), about one card every 20 seconds. Red Road, Blue Road: each race ends in 5 to 9 picks. Step minutes add up to each part's minutes.
